correctness.rationale: For ordinary locating domination it is necessary and sufficient that the selected set hit each closed neighborhood N[x] and each set {x,y} ∪ (N(x) △ N(y)). The pair condition is automatic if either vertex is selected, and otherwise says that their selected-neighbor signatures differ. I independently formed these hitting constraints and computed the upward closure of their complements' failure indicators via a Boolean subset transform: a detector mask fails exactly when its complement contains a required hitting set. The replay /workspace/independent-evidence/1.py exhausts all 2^20 masks and matches all 21 coefficients in both graphs and both models of Desargues. Totals D=362841 and P=384459; P−D has exactly (220,2460,6660,7228,3880,1050,120) at degrees 7–13. The supplied Python isomorphism certificate is a bijection with the stated adjacency test. A uniform k-set divides the coefficient by binomial(20,k); the independent deployment difference has a positive sum of Bernoulli weights for 0<p<1. At p=0 both fail; at p=1 both succeed. No authored script was executed.
residual_risks: Exact finite computation for these two graphs and labelled subsets; no assertion about other cubic graphs or the identifying-code condition.

value.rationale: Locating domination is a natural detection invariant, and the full labelled cardinality distribution is the sufficient precise data for uniform and iid detector deployment. The two canonical cubic graphs have equal order but different geometry; the exact dominance at every interior probability, and its limited support in budget, are nontrivial information beyond the known difference of minima.
residual_risks: A finite benchmark, not a general extremal theorem or empirical reliability claim for physical networks.
